d.title: Five questions the corpus cannot answer, and all five return a document
d.caption: The unanswerable set is five questions this corpus genuinely cannot answer — a competitor's integration, a SOC 2 audit scope, paying in Bitcoin. **Each one still returns a document, which is 6.2's point, and each one still returns it with a positive score.** Which is why a guard is needed at all: the retriever has no mechanism for returning nothing, so **"we found something" carries no information** and the abstention decision has to be made after retrieval by something else.

nodes.label: A question the corpus cannot answer
With a positive score
nodes.sub: in the same units as a real hit

nodes.label: So the guard is a separate decision

d.title: The sweep has no good row
d.caption: Read down the two error columns: **at 0.00 the guard answers everything and is wrong five times; at 0.40 it is wrong zero times and refuses four real questions.** There is no threshold that does both — 0.30 is the least bad at one wrong answer and one wrong refusal, and "least bad" is the honest description. Which is why §05 layers signals rather than tuning this one: **a single score cannot separate these populations well enough to pick a row you would defend.**

d.title: The populations overlap, so the second opinion is also not a decision procedure
d.caption: The cross-encoder separates the means — **−6.737 for answerable against −10.333 for unanswerable** — and then the distributions overlap in exactly the way that matters: **the worst answerable question scores −11.014 and the best unanswerable one scores −8.950.** So there is a band containing both, and any threshold inside it makes both kinds of error. A better signal moved the means and did not make the problem a classification problem with a clean boundary.

d.title: Three signals, each weak, with partly independent failures
d.caption: **Layering these is not the same as having a reliable guard** — it is accepting that each signal is weak and that their failures are partly independent. The first is the only one that **sees the context rather than a score**, and it is unenforced. The second is **free and detectable with a regex**. And AUC 0.943 on the retrieval score is **good enough to be useful and not good enough to be alone.** The honest framing: abstention is a risk-management problem, not a solved one.

cells.text: the context itself - the only one that does

d.title: Which queries actually fail, and they fail at reciprocal rank 0.00
d.caption: Not a degraded ranking — **zero**. *"I want out"* and *"the robot keeps emailing me"* return three plausible documents each and **the right one is in none of them.** Which is the population query rewriting exists for: the query shares no vocabulary with the document and dense similarity has nothing to bridge. Note they are also both phrased the way a person actually talks, which is the part a test set written by the system's author tends to miss.

d.title: The rewrite added no information — it substituted the document's words
d.caption: **The mechanism matters more than the number.** `the robot keeps emailing me` became `disable outgoing webhook notifications`, **which works because `intg-webhook-out` uses the word *webhook*.** No information was added: the user's words were replaced with the corpus's words. Which is why §03's measurement is the important one — if a rewrite works by knowing the target vocabulary, then **a rewrite written by someone who knows the corpus is not evidence that rewriting works.**

nodes.label: It works because the doc says 'webhook'

d.title: The circularity, measured: uninformed rewrites do far less
d.caption: The informed rewrite took *"I want out"* from 0.00 to **1.00**. Four plausible rewrites written **without** knowing the target document land at **0.50, 0.50, 1.00 and lower** — so rewriting genuinely helps, and **the measured benefit of an author-written rewrite overstates what a model will achieve**, because the author knows which word the document uses. The honest number is the uninformed one, and reporting the informed one is the easiest mistake to make in this lesson.

d.title: HyDE rests on 5.4's asymmetry
d.caption: A question and its answer are **different kinds of text**, so generate a plausible answer and embed **that** — because **an answer looks more like a document than a question does.** Measured here it fixes both test queries. And the caveat applies in full: **I wrote the hypothetical documents too**, so the same circularity §03 measured for rewriting applies unchanged, and the honest version of the result needs a model generating them blind.

d.title: Four techniques, and the one whose latency is serial
d.caption: Three of these add one round trip and can overlap their searches. **Decomposition cannot: if the sub-questions are dependent, the retrievals are serial**, so the latency is the sum rather than the maximum — and that is the difference between +1 round trip and +n. Which is the reason the decision about *where* to put query transformation matters: a technique that is cheap in token terms can be expensive in wall-clock, and only this column shows it.

d.title: The budget sets an effective k, whatever k you configured
d.caption: **If only three chunks fit, you are running retrieval at k=3 regardless of what the retriever was configured with.** Everything ranked fourth or below is discarded, so **the quality of the cut depends entirely on the ranking** — and the trace shows what that costs: recall is 0.571 at an effective k of 1 and does not reach 1.000 until 5. Note MRR is flat at 0.964 throughout, so **the metric that moves is the one about coverage and the metric that does not is the one about ordering.**

d.title: Ordering costs nothing, which is reason enough to do it
d.caption: Models attend less reliably to the middle of a long context, and **demonstrating that effect needs a real model** — so what the lesson presents is the ordering *arithmetic* rather than a measurement of model behaviour, and it says so. **The construction costs nothing**, which is a good reason to adopt it regardless of the effect's exact size: put the highest-scoring chunks first and last, and the ones you are least sure about in the middle where attention is weakest.

nodes.label: Attention is weaker in the middle
Measuring it needs a real model
The construction is free
nodes.sub: a sort, not a model call

nodes.label: So adopt it regardless of the size

d.title: Three budgeting mistakes, and chars-over-4 is tuned for prose
d.caption: 4.4 measured the other direction: **JSON came out at 2.23 characters per token, so the same estimate undercounts by 45%.** The rule is that the heuristic is tuned for English prose and **fails on anything structured** — JSON, code, tables, identifiers, non-Latin scripts. And an undercount is the dangerous direction: **it means a request that gets rejected or truncated** rather than one that is merely smaller than it could be.

d.title: Three ways a citation goes wrong, and only two are catchable for free
d.caption: The first is correct. The second cites `data-policy`, **a document that was never retrieved — caught by a regex against the context, for nothing.** The third is the hard one: it cites `auth-session`, which **was** retrieved, and the claim it supports is not in it. **A structural check passes it**, because the id is real and present — so detecting it requires reading the document, which is §02's model call.

d.title: The proxy does not work, which is more useful than if it had
d.caption: The proper check is natural-language inference — does the document **entail** the sentence. No NLI model was available, so the lesson uses the cross-encoder as a relevance proxy **and labels it as such.** The result is that **the proxy does not work**, and that is a more useful outcome than a success would have been: it establishes that **relevance and entailment are different questions**, so the component you would reach for does not do the job. A real check needs an entailment model or a model prompted to judge support with the document in front of it — **either way a model call.**

nodes.label: Use the cross-encoder as a proxy
So: an NLI model, or a prompted judge

d.title: Four checks, three of them free or cheap
d.caption: The layering is the practical answer to §02's cost problem: **run the free checks on every answer and the expensive one on a sample or on the ones the free checks flagged.** The first two cost a regex. The third — every sentence making a factual claim carries a citation — is cheap and catches the common case of a grounded first paragraph followed by three ungrounded ones. Only per-claim entailment needs a model, and it is the only one that catches §01's third row.

d.title: Three indexes, three different things a delete does
d.caption: **`IndexFlatIP`'s `remove_ids` shifts the array, so ids after the deleted one renumber** — and if your document metadata is aligned positionally, every document after the deletion now points at the wrong text. **That the course's own exercises use positional alignment is the point**: it is correct for a fixed corpus and becomes a defect the moment the corpus can change, which is a reasonable summary of this whole lesson.
cells: tombstone and filter at query time

d.title: A nightly rebuild means an edit's staleness depends on the hour it was made
d.caption: With one rebuild at 02:00, **an edit at 02:05 is served stale for 23 hours 55 minutes and an edit at 23:45 for 2 hours 15 minutes.** Same policy, same system, **a 10× difference in exposure decided by when somebody happened to click save.** Which is the argument for stating a staleness *window* rather than a rebuild *frequency*: the frequency sounds like a guarantee and the window is the number a user experiences.

d.title: All three drift gradually, with no error and slightly worse recall
d.caption: Each index degrades under incremental updates for its own reason. **BM25's `df`, `avgdl` and `N` are corpus-wide, so every IDF is computed from stale counts** — and 6.3 showed IDF is where BM25's behaviour lives. **IVF assigns new documents to the nearest *old* centroid.** HNSW's graph is built by insertion order, so churn leaves worse connectivity than a rebuild. **The same silent-failure shape as 5.4's un-normalised vectors and 5.2's scrambled PDF columns** — which is the argument for a periodic rebuild even when incremental updates work exactly as designed.

items.sub: df, avgdl and N are corpus-wide, so every IDF is stale

items.label: IVF
items.sub: new documents go to the nearest OLD centroid

items.label: HNSW
items.sub: the graph is built by insertion order; churn worsens connectivity

d.title: The cheapest freshness signal is a date in the citation
d.caption: `[data-retention, updated 2024-03-11]` — **the document's own timestamp, carried into the answer.** It costs one metadata field and one formatting change, and it does something no monitoring can: **it makes staleness visible to the person who can judge whether it matters.** A user reading a policy answer dated eight months ago knows to check; the same user reading an undated answer does not know there was anything to check.

nodes.label: To the person who can judge it
Undated, there is nothing to check
nodes.sub: and no way to know that

d.title: The payload arrives in the same channel as the instruction it contradicts
d.caption: 5.7 measured where retrieved context lands: **inside the *system* message, alongside the real instructions.** So an injected instruction in a document arrives **in the same channel as the instruction it is contradicting**, separated only by formatting **that the model has no architectural reason to respect.** Which is why every defence in §03 is labelled *not enforced*: there is no mechanism that marks one span of a single string as inert.

nodes.label: A document with an appended payload

d.title: The payload changes the similarity by 0.0126, which is nothing to threshold on
d.caption: Appending the attack to an otherwise unchanged document moves the cosine from **0.7394 to 0.7267 — a drop of 0.0126.** Which is the finding: **there is nothing to filter on.** That difference is smaller than the ordinary variation between legitimate results for the same query, so any threshold that caught it would reject real documents at a far higher rate. The attack is not hidden; it is simply **not anomalous in the space you are searching.**

d.title: Two defences that hold, and both work by removing a possibility
d.caption: **Filter what enters the context at all**: 5.5's metadata filter is a **structural** guarantee — the document is not retrieved, so its instructions are never read, **and that works regardless of how persuasive the payload is.** And **bound what a compromised turn can do**: if the model has no tool that sends email, *"exfiltrate the data"* is **a sentence it cannot act on.** This is 3.6's least-privilege argument reached from the security side, and the two together are the only entries in §03's table not marked *not enforced.*

d.title: You cannot detect the injection; you can detect its effects
d.caption: **It is natural language, and any pattern you block can be rephrased** — so prevention is not available. The effects are cheap to detect and **all four signals are output-side**: a missing or unretrieved citation, an answer that contradicts its own context, an unexpected tool call, an output containing something that looks like an address or a key. **5.7's citation requirement is what makes the first one computable** — and that is the auditability argument for the third time in this module: you cannot prevent the behaviour, so **require an output that makes it visible.**

nodes.label: An unexpected tool call
nodes.sub: or a key-shaped string in the output

nodes.label: Require an output that is auditable

d.title: The usable row is a high threshold and a low hit rate
d.caption: Read the sweep for its usable row rather than its summary statistic. **At 0.40 the cache serves 8 wrong answers. At 0.90 it serves zero and misses five of eight genuine repeats.** A high threshold and a low hit rate is **the correct operating point when one of your two errors is telling a user something false** — and §03 is why those two errors cannot be traded off against each other on a single axis.

d.title: A miss costs latency; a wrong hit is a specific false statement
d.caption: **A miss costs latency** — you do work you would have done anyway and the user gets a correct answer slightly later. **A wrong hit serves a confidently wrong answer to a different question, with a citation, and the user has no way to tell.** *"Is retention 30 days"* answered from the entry for *"is retention 90 days"* is not a degraded answer: it is **a specific false statement about a data policy, delivered with a citation to a real document, to a user who asked a precise question.**

nodes.label: A miss
nodes.sub: the work you would have done

nodes.label: With a citation to a real document
And no way for the user to tell
nodes.sub: so they are not comparable errors

d.title: Three caches carry no risk, and they are keyed on exact text
d.caption: The pattern is visible down the key column: **the three safe caches are keyed on exact text and the dangerous one is keyed on an embedding.** Exact keying cannot join two different questions, which is the entire source of §03's risk. And the reranker-score row is the one worth taking first: **~1362 ms saved, keyed on a (query, document) pair, with stale documents as the only failure mode** — the best ratio of saving to risk anywhere in this module.

d.title: Two expiry conditions, and almost nobody implements the second
d.caption: A cached answer **was grounded in documents that can change** (7.5), so it has **two** expiry conditions: **time, which everyone implements**, and **source change — any cited document was edited or deleted — which almost nobody does.** And 5.7's citation requirement is what makes the second one computable at all: the cache entry knows which documents it depended on, so a document edit can invalidate exactly the entries that cited it.

nodes.label: The entry knows what it cited
So an edit invalidates exactly those

d.title: Three architectures for images and tables
d.caption: Three genuinely different answers to the same problem. **A shared embedding space** searches both modalities at once and needs a model trained for it. **Describe-then-embed** writes a text description with a vision model, embeds the **description**, stores the original and returns the original — so every stored vector comes from one text model and every comparison is text-to-text. And **page-as-image** stops extracting anything, which removes chunking and parsing along with the problem.
cells: one space, both modalities, searched together

cells.text: embed the description, return the original

cells: a vision call per asset, once
treat each page as an image, many vectors

d.title: Why describe-then-embed is the default
d.caption: It is usually presented as the pragmatic compromise and it is better than that: **once every stored vector comes from one text model, every comparison is text-to-text in one space** — so there is no modality gap to calibrate, no cross-modal score to reconcile, and none of 6.4's incomparable-scale problem arrives in a new form. The cost is **a vision call per asset at index time, paid once**, against a retrieval-time cost that the other two architectures carry on every query.

nodes.label: A vision model describes each asset
No modality gap to calibrate
nodes.sub: and no 6.4 in a new form

nodes.label: Cost paid once, not per query
nodes.sub: which the others do not do

d.title: What to cache, ordered by saving per unit of risk
d.caption: 7.7's table, read as a deployment decision. **Reranker scores are the standout: ~1362 ms saved for a (query, document) key whose only failure mode is staleness.** Query embeddings and retrieval results are smaller savings at zero and near-zero risk. And the answer cache is last on this list rather than absent from it — it saves everything and it is the one with a wrong-answer failure mode, so it needs 7.7's high threshold and §05's source-change invalidation.

d.title: What to precompute, which is everything that does not depend on the query
d.caption: The dividing line is clean: **anything computable without the query belongs at index time.** Document embeddings, the BM25 statistics, the index structure itself, chunk-level metadata, and any vision descriptions from 7.8 — all of it is query-independent and therefore paid once rather than per request. Which is also why 7.5 matters: **everything on that list is a cached derivative of the corpus, so every one of them goes stale when the corpus changes.**

d.title: What degrades first under load, and each step has a measured cost
d.caption: A degradation ladder is only honest if each rung has a number attached, and these do. **Lowering `fetch_k` costs exact-term MRR — 6.7 measured it falling from 1.000 to 0.875 at fetch 10.** Dropping the reranker returns that class to **0.781**. Loosening the cache raises 7.7's wrong-answer rate, which is the rung to take last because it is the only one that trades correctness rather than quality.

d.title: The one that is free: more stages, half the latency
d.caption: `dense + rerank` is **1.456 s a query**. `hybrid + mmr + rerank` — **three more stages** — is **0.717 s**, less than half. This is 6.8's finding stated as a deployment fact rather than an ablation result: **MMR narrows the candidate set before the cross-encoder runs, so the expensive stage does fewer forward passes**, and the cheap stages that enable that cost a handful of dot products. **The only optimisation in this module that costs nothing and trades nothing.**
